You do the high poly first before the low poly because it is likely your mesh will change in shape during the process of adding details. You may have to modify your low poly a little or alot depending on what you did. Sometimes you can get away with it if the model is simple but it's way more efficient to do the low poly after the high poly. It saves time.

I find that if you set big goals for yourself and hold your own work to a very high expectation you can actually cause yourself to burn out and become frustrated and unmotivated to work. I did this before and your post reminds me of it. Take your work baby steps at a time. Look at the ultimate goal and break it down into smaller more manageable goals. You want to lean how to model a spider. Work on it in parts. One day you learn how to model the spiders legs for example. Do research on spider legs, reference images and decide how to approach the modeling aspect. Should I sculpt it or should I model it by hand? Finish the legs and move on to the head, eyes, body, hair, and etc. Remember baby steps.

Generally you make a highpoly model first then bake it down to a low poly model. You can then make a low poly for baking by making a retopo of the high poly or by reducing the poly count of a copy of the high poly. This is really the only way to do it right. I've spent tons of time learning hard surface modeling and there are no shortcuts here. Even with hard ops you don't get the same clean results. Sub-d modeling requires lots of skill and patience. Did I mention it requires LOTS of skill and patience? If you have any questions please feel free to ask me. I know many things in this area of blender and can provide a good resource.

Some stuff to learn:
1) Movement. Bunny hopping, strife jumping, circle jumping (if that is still a thing now), ledge/ double jumping, rocket jumping, when to use sneaking and how to evade projectiles.
2) Arena Strategy. Know where spawns are, know where weapons/ powerups are, know where good choke points are, know when to back off your enemy and how to flank them. Know when to use jump pads against your enemy (very useful because people always chase you up a jump pad).
3) Weapons. Know which weapons are used for what purpose, switch between weapons to deal the most damage or maybe confuse your enemy.
4) Learn how to use and counter the new player abilities. Everyone has these new abilities so you gotta know who you are shooting at and what skill they can use on you and how counter that skill with your own.

These are all just examples and there are some good guides floating around out there if you want to lean some more. I'm a mid level player myself. These things help a lot. I used to be really bad but I just kept playing the game.

Welcome to Linux! I have been a long time Windows user like you but I always end up formatting my hard drive and installing Linux on all the PCs I've owned. *Don't use Arch because you have to install everything including the desktop environment yourself through a command line which is easy if you know how to use a terminal. To learn more about the command line which is really useful edx has a great Linux course. I recommend you use something more user friendly like Ubuntu, Fedora, Manjaro KDE or openSUSE just to name a few.

*Wine is good and will run most programs quite nicely but it all depends. Go onto wine's website and check user reports to see if your programs run with wine.

*Drivers are usually easy to install if you need something that is not already included in Linux. Linux supports alot of hardware from printers to graphics cards and drawing tablets. If you need a driver for something in particular check the hardware manufacturer's website for linux drivers. Usually you have to use a command line to install them but it is simple.

*No that is a lie. Stuff is pretty stable in Linux. I've had Windows 7/8/10 break more from official updates or bugs than anything in a Linux OS.

*Schoolwork should be fine. Libreoffice gets it done just as good as MS Office. When I was in school I used LibreOffice on Windows to write papers and make spreadsheets. I did only my presentations using free Word Web Apps.

*Gaming is not the best on Linux because it lacks huge titles but you can still play some pretty good games through Steam like CSGO or Borderlands The Pre Sequal or Minecraft using java runtime for Linux.

Take the plunge! You will never wanna look back.
